My view is that moms should raise their own kids, inside a community where the care is really shared. The village can handle meals, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, and a lot of the fathering, but it should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.

A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. It's one outsider's interpretation of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing what she saw, but it's still a powerful picture. She talks about how the babies are carried with them and brought into adult life, how the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and how it doesn't fall on one tired parent to be their whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.

Experiments where kids don't sleep and live with their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that they ended the practice of kids sleeping communally for a mix of reasons: developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care and many loving adults in their lives, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.

I'd suggest taking a direct look at what's going on at Tamera's Children's Place instead of caricaturing it. To be honest, my own bias is still toward a system where kids interact with more people, without the parent-child bond being made ideologically inconvenient.
community-s8i1/u1.A:
It's a fine point, but IMO the balance only works with mothers raising their own kids, and the village helping out with food, watching, teaching, protecting, playing, even some of the fathering, but not taking the kids away from their mothers to "liberate" them.

The reason children need a community around them is covered well in Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept, which is her (possibly rose-colored) view of the Ye'kuana tribe from her vantage point as an outsider. In short, the babies are carried around with them and included in adult life, and the kids are surrounded by people of various ages and are able to learn by participating. While some of this can be faked in a nuclear household, it would be much better in a village.

As for experiments with kids not sleeping and living with their parents, I think extreme caution is called for. From what I've read, the Israeli kibbutzim stopped letting their kids sleep in the communal kids' place for a variety of reasons, including research into how it affected the kids' development, how the parents felt about it, and changing social conditions. Kids can certainly benefit from high-quality group care and from having more people in their lives, but I don't think it should replace solid attachments to their parents.

It might be worth investigating what they're doing at the Children's Place in Tamera to see if it's what I think it is, though of course I'm biased for a system where the kids are interacting with more people.
community-s8i1/u1.B:
Yes! I don't think that there is any question that mothers should raise their own children, but with the help of the whole village. Being raised by the village does not necessarily mean that a child has to be taken away from the mother. The village can help feed the child, watch the child, teach the child, protect the child, play with the child, father the child etc. without taking the child away from the mother.

One reason why having a village or a large community raise the child is very important, can be found in The Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff. This book is an 'outsider's' views on the Ye'kuana tribe (it's possible that she is glorifying them) but I found the aspects of carrying the babies with them everywhere they go, bringing the babies into their life, having many different ages of people around the children all the time and allowing the children to learn by participating in the life of the community extremely beneficial. While a lot of this can be accomplished within a nuclear household, it is much easier to do this in a village.

However, I would be very careful about experimenting with kids not sleeping/ living with their parents. The Israeli kibbutzim stopped allowing kids to sleep in the communal sleeping place for a variety of reasons. (research on the kibbutzim will tell about the developmental aspects, but it was also due to parents not wanting it any more and a change in the society of the kibbutzim). I think that kids can benefit from the high quality group care that they would receive at a place such as Tamera's Children's Place, but I am still biased toward kids being around lots of people.

If anyone is interested in learning more about Tamera's Children's Place, I'd suggest checking it out.

community-s8i1/u2.input:
The Amish let their young people make the decision to join the church on their own when they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining. Pop culture makes Rumspringa seem far wilder and more universal than it is, but it's still a big deal that they're baptized as adults, because then belonging is a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If the kids never leave, the community has no way of knowing whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, see other ways of living, and disagree with the founders, without treating them as traitors for it.

Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.

The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. Kids who grow up without ever using money especially need a decent education in how the money world operates, and what to do when they have to deal with it: jobs, rent, contracts, banks, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help.

They also need a good set of transferable skills and education, good relationships with people outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community). It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, travel expenses, tools or a little money, but even if it can't, it can at least not make things worse by punishing people for leaving, or by holding back knowledge or records a young adult would need to function outside the community. No upbringing can provide perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.

It's possible that some of them will split off, either permanently, or into their own communities with different values, rather than wait decades to inherit the original one. And parents may experience that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.
community-s8i1/u2.A:
Do note that the Amish allow their children to leave, and that even after being permitted to behave however they want as adults a very large majority of them (85% or higher, apparently) choose to join the Amish church. Yes, the Rumspringa is not as wild as pop culture would have it, but the fact that they’re joining as adults is no small thing.

Conversely, if they’re not allowed to leave how would the Amish know that they want to join? Allow the children to study and travel and make friends outside of the group. It’s okay for them to see other ways of doing things, and it’s okay for them to think that the founders might have been wrong about something. Don’t treat them like traitors for it.

A lot of this is going to depend on what the parents are like during the child’s childhood, because the earlier that options are foreclosed the harder it is to take advantage of them later. Obviously most people aren’t going to give their kids a bunch of money to travel the world when they turn 18, and are going to want to have some viable next step for them, but it’s something to think about. Also relevant is whether or not the community has money; if they’re poor or avoid using money it’ll be harder to give them money, and also more of them are probably going to be focused on basic survival issues like food and medical care.

Still, at the very least it shouldn’t be artificially difficult for people to leave. If the kids aren’t allowed to use money, they should be well-educated on how to function in a money-based society (because that’s the one they’ll have to enter if they leave).

The kids should also be well-educated generally, with skills that will be useful even if they leave, good relationships with potential non-community members, easy access to their records and other documents, and some reasonable next step they can take (school, apprenticeship, work, family, other community, etc.) Ideally there’d be some community resources that can help with their transition (housing, travel expenses, tools, money, etc.), but if that’s not possible at least don’t make things harder by punishing people for leaving, or refusing to give them the knowledge or records they’ll need to survive. Obviously there’s going to be some path-dependence here, but it shouldn’t be too hard.

Of course, this does run the risk of people splitting off either permanently or into their own communities with different values, rather than waiting until everyone’s dead and taking over the community. That might not be great for the parents, but…
community-s8i1/u2.B:
It's interesting that the Amish allow their children the freedom to choose to join the church when they're older, and still see 85% (or is it more?) of them join. While the Rumspringa isn't as universal or crazy as pop culture makes it out to be, it's still a big deal that they're not forced into joining and are instead baptized as adults.

If they don't let the kids leave, how will they know if the kids would come back on their own? Let the kids study and travel and make friends. If they want to see other ways of doing things, let them. If they don't agree with the way the founders did things, don't call them traitors.

The problem is, everyone's kids are going to be somewhat limited in their choices based on their upbringing. Very few people are going to, upon their kid's 18th birthday, just give them a bunch of money and say "here, go see the world". Most people are going to help their kids prepare to do something that actually works. And if the movement is based on being poor or not having money, they probably won't have much to give the kids, since they'll be more focused on food and medical care and survival.

So instead of holding it to an impossible standard, let's hold it to a standard that's actually possible: don't make it artificially impossible for people to leave. If they don't let the kids use money, let the kids learn about how the money-world works. If they leave, they need to know how to function in a money-world.

Also, when they leave, they should have some generally applicable skills - don't teach them something that only works within the movement. They should have a good education. They should have relations with people outside the movement. They should have all of their records. They should have somewhere to go - whether it's school, or a job, or an apprentice-ship, or family, or another community. It would be nice if they had some resources to help make the transition easier, but if they're a poor community, they may not have the resources. At the very least, they shouldn't make it more difficult than it has to be - don't punish people for leaving, don't withhold records or knowledge from them. It's impossible to not have some path dependancy in a movement, but it's possible to not trap people in a movement.

Oh, and they might split off either permanently or into their own communities with different values, instead of waiting to inherit the original movement in a few decades.

community-s8i2/u1.A:
First of all, I don't see that it is taking the kids away from the moms. I believe that moms should raise their kids, but I don't see why it can't be done in a more communal fashion. I'd like to see a "village" take care of the kids, including things like meal provision, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, and even a lot of the fathering if needed. But I don't think that this should be used as an excuse to take the kids away from the mom in the name of "liberation".

There are a lot of good reasons to have more of a "community" with the kids. If I were to recommend one book to read about a good example (admittedly interpreted by a non-native, and perhaps romanticized) of community with kids, I'd recommend The Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff, about the Ye'kuana . Things like carrying the kids (even as babies) along with everyone else, having the kids surrounded by people of a variety of ages, letting them participate in what's going on, and not putting the social burden on one individual (normally a parent) are things that could be done (at least partially) in a nuclear household, but would be much easier in a "village".

On the other hand, "experiments" with kids not sleeping with their parents and perhaps not living with their parents should be taken with great caution. From what I can tell, the Israeli Kibbutz have stopped their practice of kids sleeping together (not with their parents) for a variety of reasons, including apparent developmental research , the wishes of the kids' parents , and perhaps other social changes . This doesn't mean that kids can't get great benefit from high-quality communal care, and from having a large number of people love them, but that it shouldn't replace secure attachment to their parents.

Finally, it might be helpful to check out Tamera's Children's Place and see what they're doing. In a way, I'm still biased towards having the kids interact with more people.
community-s8i2/u1.B:
I disagree that the mother should not raise her own child. I agree that the child should be raised by the mother in the context of a village, where the village helps with feeding, watching, teaching, protecting, playing with, even fathering the child, but not by taking the child away from the mother in the name of "liberating" her.

One reason I think kids need a "village" to raise them is described by Jean Liedloff in "The Continuum Concept", where she describes (as an outsider) the lifestyle of the Yekuana tribe. (Yes, she idealizes them, but still...) The babies are carried around and included in the adult's life. The children are surrounded by people of multiple ages and participate in what's going on around them. It doesn't fall to one parent to entertain the child and provide all of his social interaction. This can be somewhat mimicked in a nuclear household, but a village is better.

Experiments where kids don't sleep with and live with their parents should be undertaken with caution. I read that the Israeli kibbutzim stopped letting the kids sleep in the communal kids' place for a variety of reasons, not the least of which was research on child development, but also because the parents wanted to and because times were changing. It seems to me that kids could get a lot out of a high-quality communal living situation where they'd be exposed to lots of loving adults, but it shouldn't be at the expense of letting them form secure attachments with their parents.

It might be helpful to look at what Tamera's Children's Place is actually doing. I'm biased in favor of kids having lots of people to interact with.

community-s8i2/u2.A:
It occurs to that the Amish let their kids basically grow up however they want, and then decide whether to join the church when they're old enough. It doesn't seem like everybody goes as wild as pop culture would make it seem with their Rumspringa , but either way it sounds like 85% or more do join up when they get older. This is pretty cool because it means that they are choosing to join when they're older, and so their baptism is actually meaningful.

In contrast, if they weren't allowed to leave at all, there'd be no way for the kids to show that they'd stay if allowed to leave, so might as well let them leave. Let them study and travel and make friends. If they want to not follow in the footsteps of the founder, that's okay, don't call them traitors.

But the problem is that growing up in any community limits what people can do in the future. And most people aren't going to just give their kid a bunch of money and say "here, go see the world for a while" when they turn 18. They're going to try to prepare them for something they can actually do. And if the community is poor or doesn't use money, then they may not even have the money, or may have more important things to spend it on like food and medical care.

So, what can they do, within the realm of possibility, to make sure that their children would be able to leave if they wanted to? At the very least, they should not do anything to artificially prevent their children from leaving. If the kids don't use money, they should be educated about how to use money in the money-world, what to do when they leave, etc.

They should also be educated in more generally useful skills, be allowed to form relationships outside of the community, be given access to all of their records, etc, and have at least one thing they could plausibly do once they leave the community. It would also be good to give them resources to help them leave (housing, travel, money, etc), but if the community doesn't have those, that's okay. On the other hand, it's easy not to make things worse, so at least don't punish people for leaving, and don't hold back knowledge or records. It's impossible to eliminate path dependance entirely, but it's possible to not be a cult.

Also, they should probably allow splitting into new communities with different values, either permanently, or before inheriting the community in a few decades. This may be what the parents are afraid of.
community-s8i2/u2.B:
The Amish solve this by letting the children join when they are old enough to make their own decision. That doesn’t mean it is the wild party time that pop culture makes Rumspringa out to be, but enough that it works: over 85% of Amish join the church. It also means that they join as adults, which makes a big difference.

If the kids never “left”, there’s no way to tell if they would come back. Let the kids study, travel, make friends, and even disagree with the founders. It might seem like they are traitors, but…

Everyone’s childhoods limit their future options. Most of the population probably won’t give their kid a bag of cash when they turn 18 and let them go see the world. It’s silly to expect them to prepare for something that won’t happen. Especially if they’re poor or don’t use money, their main concern should be to make sure their kids can eat, get medical care, and otherwise survive.

So let’s aim for something more reasonable: not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. If the kids don’t use money, make sure they get a good education on how money works and how to operate in a moneyed society.

Make sure they get a good education and have good skills that will work outside the movement, and good relationships with non-movement people who can help them. Give them their records, documents, etc., and make sure they have somewhere to go (school, apprenticeship, job, family, other community, etc.). It would be good to give them resources to help them transition (place to stay, travel cost, tools, money, etc.) but if they don’t have that, at least don’t make it worse (don’t punish them for leaving, don’t refuse to give them information/records they need to function, etc.). It won’t be perfect and there will be path dependence, but it’s a start.

It might be that they’ll split off either individually or into their own communities with different values, rather than waiting until everyone dies to take over the movement, but at least the parents will be gone anyway.
